meta.title: Who really said "In individuals, insanity is rare; but in groups, parties, nations and epochs, it is the rule"? | Quotle.info

meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In individuals, insanity is rare; but in groups, parties, nations and epochs, it is the rule'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Nietzsche: aphorism 156 of Beyond Good and Evil (1886). The famous English wording is a light reordering of Helen Zimmern's public-domain translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Nietzsche — this is aphorism 156 of the “Epigrams and Interludes” (Sprüche und Zwischenspiele) in Beyond Good and Evil (1886). The German reads “Der Irrsinn ist bei Einzelnen etwas Seltenes, — aber bei Gruppen, Parteien, Völkern, Zeiten die Regel.” The popular English simply reorders the opening of Helen Zimmern’s public-domain translation, whose second half (“in groups, parties, nations, and epochs it is the rule”) it matches word for word.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Beyond Good and Evil (Jenseits von Gut und Böse)

source.excerpt: Insanity in individuals is something rare — but in groups, parties, nations, and epochs, it is the rule.
trail: The German original appears as aphorism 156 in Wikiquote’s sourced page for Beyond Good and Evil: “Der Irrsinn ist bei Einzelnen etwas Seltenes … die Regel.”
Wikisource’s full text of Part IV gives Helen Zimmern’s wording: “Insanity in individuals is something rare — but in groups, parties, nations, and epochs, it is the rule.”
The complete Zimmern translation is on Project Gutenberg, confirming the aphorism belongs to a pre-1931, public-domain English edition.
source.excerptNote: Aphorism 156, in Helen Zimmern’s public-domain translation. The version that circulates online (“In individuals, insanity is rare; but in groups …”) reorders only the opening clause; the German original is “Der Irrsinn ist bei Einzelnen etwas Seltenes, — aber bei Gruppen, Parteien, Völkern, Zeiten die Regel.”

sourceLink.text: Beyond Good and Evil, Part IV (Helen Zimmern translation)

source.rightsNote: Both the underlying work and the standard English rendering are in the public domain in the United States: the German original was published in 1886, and Helen Zimmern’s English translation appeared in 1907 — both well before 1931. Note that later copyrighted translations (e.g. Walter Kaufmann, 1966; R. J. Hollingdale) phrase the aphorism differently (“madness … peoples … ages”).

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and former classical philologist whose work on morality, nihilism, and the psychology of belief reshaped modern thought. Beyond Good and Evil (1886) is one of his mature works, and its fourth part, “Epigrams and Interludes,” is a run of aphorisms — of which this remark on the madness of crowds is number 156.

misattribution.heading: The wording, sorted out
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is correct — this really is Nietzsche. The only thing worth flagging is the wording: the famous English line is a lightly reworded version of the published translations, and it is almost never cited to a specific source.

items.who: An internet rewording of Helen Zimmern’s translation
items.why: No standard published translation opens “In individuals, insanity is rare.” Zimmern’s 1907 text reads “Insanity in individuals is something rare — but in groups, parties, nations, and epochs, it is the rule.” The viral version simply flips the first clause; the second half is identical.

Later versions differ in vocabulary rather than meaning — e.g. Hollingdale’s “Madness is something rare in individuals — but in groups, parties, peoples, epochs it is the rule.” Choice of “insanity/madness” and “nations/peoples” is a translator’s decision, not a change of source.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: really Nietzsche, really Beyond Good and Evil, aphorism 156 (1886). The quoted English just reorders the opening of the public-domain translation.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The remark sits inside a chapter of one-line epigrams, and it distills a recurring Nietzschean suspicion of the herd: that reason is an individual achievement and rarely a collective one. Detached from that setting, it now travels as a standalone verdict on mobs, parties, and mass movements.
Because the thought is genuinely his and the phrasing only lightly altered, the line is that unusual thing among viral ‘quotes’ — a real one, drifting only in its exact words.
